title: A fraud model that never looks
hook: A fraud model that never looks at a payment. How accurate can it be?

knows: that a model can label things right or wrong
doesNotKnow: that accuracy hides what happens to a rare class

misconception: A model with 99% accuracy is a good model.
objective: The learner can explain that when one class is rare, a model that ignores it scores high accuracy, that a model catching most of the rare cases can score lower, and that you must ask how many of the cases you care about it catches.

claims.text: The toy has 1,000 card payments, 10 of them fraud (1%); the 1% rate is invented for the lesson.
claims.source: The lesson's own data in Demo.tsx (TOTAL = 1000, 10 entries in FRAUD_RANKS).

claims.text: Accuracy is the share of payments the model labels correctly. Approving everything is right on all 990 genuine payments and wrong on all 10 frauds: 990 / 1,000 = 99.0%, with 0 of 10 frauds caught.
claims.source: Arithmetic; reproduced by running score(0) from Demo.tsx: accuracy 0.99, caught 0.

claims.text: The slider flags payments in order of an invented, fixed risk ranking. Flagging the riskiest 20 catches 8 of the 10 frauds and wrongly flags 12 genuine payments, for an accuracy of 98.6%, lower than approving everything; the reveal quotes the first setting the learner reached where accuracy fell below 99.0%.
claims.source: score(20) from Demo.tsx (FRAUD_RANKS = 0, 1, 3, 5, 8, 11, 15, 19, 28, 44): caught 8, false alarms 12, accuracy (8 + 978) / 1000 = 0.986. Reproduced with a separate script that runs the lesson's model code. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Own enumeration of score() for 0-50: n=20 gives 8 caught, 12 false alarms, 0.986. First setting below 99.0% is 11 if the learner slides one step at a time; the reveal quotes seen, which matches the claim text.

claims.text: With any ranking, flagging only payments that turn out to be fraud raises accuracy, and every genuine payment flagged lowers it by 0.1 point; so catching fraud and keeping accuracy above 99% pull against each other in this toy. The stage says 'Catches still outnumber false alarms' while accuracy is above 99.0% with some payments flagged.
claims.source: accuracy = (caught + 990 − false alarms) / 1000, from score() in Demo.tsx. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): accuracy = (990 + caught - false alarms)/1000, so it is above 99.0% exactly when caught > false alarms; checked for every slider value 0-50.

claims.text: About real systems: card-fraud data are heavily imbalanced; one widely used public data set has 492 frauds among 284,807 card transactions (about 0.17%).
claims.source: Dal Pozzolo, Caelen, Johnson & Bontempi 2015, “Calibrating Probability with Undersampling for Unbalanced Classification”, IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (the ULB credit-card fraud data set, September 2013 European cardholders); He & Garcia 2009, “Learning from Imbalanced Data”, IEEE TKDE 21(9), lists fraud detection among imbalanced problems.

recall.question: A disease screen is 98% accurate in a town where 2% of people have the disease. What should you ask before trusting it?
options: How many of the sick people it actually catches
recall.why: Calling everyone healthy would already score 98%. When one class is rare, accuracy can hide that the model misses it; check its hits on the rare class.
